title: How to Build a Customer-Back CPG Company
gist: BCG argues the brand-led CPG commercial model is structurally exhausted — 2020-2024 industry value rose 18% while volume fell 1.4%, retailers now control over two-thirds of FMCG sales in the UK, France and Germany, and retailer-side AI has erased the manufacturer's information advantage. The proposed fix is a 'customer-back' operating model built backward from three retailer decision points (category story, joint business plan, joint performance review), with cross-functional customer pods, a single data platform and agentic AI flipping key-account time from ~70% internal prep to ~80% customer-facing, worth a claimed 1-3 percentage points of annual revenue.

insights.claim: Consumer packaged goods growth from 2020 to 2024 was almost entirely price-driven: industry value grew 18% while volume fell 1.4%, meaning the pricing lever that carried the last cycle is now largely spent.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: CPG top-line comps that still lean on price/mix rather than volume should be treated as low-quality growth; screen for companies with positive volume mix before paying a defensive-staples multiple.
insights.quote: as GlobalData Plc reports, from 2020 to 2024, industry value grew 18% while volume fell 1.4%
insights.locator: A Difficult Environment for Consumer Goods

insights.claim: The fast-moving consumer goods sector has underperformed most major industries on shareholder returns for much of the past decade, with growth that is slower, more expensive and more unpredictable than in prior cycles.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Undermines the 'staples as safe compounder' default; the sector needs an operating-model catalyst, not just multiple re-rating, to close the TSR gap.
insights.quote: The fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector has underperformed most major industries on shareholder returns for much of the past decade.
insights.locator: Company. The fast-moving consumer goods sector

insights.claim: 81% of shoppers reported high concern about the cost of essentials in 2025, and roughly 30% to 40% of consumers are buying more from discounters and choosing more affordable brands, driving sustained outflow from branded products to retailer private label.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Private-label share gain is framed as a persistent value-perception shift, not a cyclical trade-down — bearish for mid-tier branded portfolios, supportive for discounter and private-label-heavy retail formats.
insights.quote: around 30% to 40% of consumers are buying more from discounters and choosing more affordable brands
insights.locator: Consumer. Inflation and price sensitivity are rising

insights.claim: Category stagnation in CPG is being driven simultaneously by household budget pressure, a shift toward simpler diets and health-focused behaviors, and mission-driven values-based purchasing — while omnichannel and e-commerce migration raises marketing, customer-acquisition, logistics and fulfilment costs.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Demand generation is getting structurally more expensive at the same time volumes flatten — watch gross-to-net and A&P efficiency as the real margin battleground, not headline pricing.
insights.quote: Generating demand is therefore becoming more costly due to higher marketing costs and customer- acquisition costs and the rising demands of logistics and fulfilment.
insights.locator: Category. Today, CPG organizations are experiencing category stagnation

themes.theme: Retailer power and the lost information edge

insights.claim: Top retailers in several major European markets including the UK, France and Germany now account for more than two-thirds of FMCG sales, creating concentrated price-exposure risk for manufacturers whose own organizations are fragmented across geographies.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Bargaining-power asymmetry favors European grocery retailers over branded suppliers in annual negotiations; expect continued supplier margin concession risk in EU trade terms.
insights.quote: The top retailers in many European markets, including the UK, France, and Germany, account for more than two-thirds of FMCG sales, according to our research.
insights.locator: Customer. Retailers' bargaining power is growing.

insights.claim: International retail buying groups have added a new layer of negotiating pressure because prices or terms a manufacturer agrees in one country can be referenced against it across several other countries.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Cross-border price arbitrage compresses a manufacturer's ability to run differentiated country pricing — a structural drag on European CPG realized price that is rarely modeled explicitly.
insights.quote: prices or terms agreed in one country may be referenced across several others
insights.locator: International retail buying groups have added a new layer

insights.claim: Retailers now deploy their own AI to continuously scan pricing, promotions, inventory and demand, compressing category reviews that once took weeks into hours, so retailer analytics increasingly rival or surpass those of their manufacturer partners.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: The classic CPG moat — superior category and shopper data sold into the retailer — is eroding; AI spend at retailers is a competitive weapon against suppliers, not just a cost-efficiency story.
insights.quote: The information advantage that once belonged to CPG companies has therefore largely evaporated
insights.locator: Retailers are also becoming markedly more sophisticated.

insights.claim: A manufacturer that arrives at a retailer meeting with siloed functional inputs rather than an integrated, evidence-based proposal now negotiates from a structurally weaker position than it did a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Commercial-model integration is becoming a determinant of realized trade terms — a differentiator between CPG peers that will show up in gross margin before it shows up in share.
insights.locator: a manufacturer that shows up with siloed inputs

insights.claim: Relying on negotiation pressure or push tactics to secure shelf space now delivers diminishing returns and can escalate into outright product de-listings.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: De-listing risk is the tail event to watch in supplier-retailer standoffs; distribution losses are harder to reverse than price concessions.
insights.quote: relying on negotiation pressure or push tactics to get products on the shelf delivers diminishing returns and can even risk product de-listings
insights.locator: Build a North Star strategy.

themes.theme: The internal-gravity tax on commercial capability

insights.claim: Key account managers and frontline sales in CPG can spend around 70% of their time preparing internally for buyer meetings rather than selling, and only a fraction of their time in front of the customer.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Quantifies a large, addressable productivity pool inside branded CPG — the single clearest lever for SG&A-neutral revenue improvement and a natural target for AI deployment.
insights.quote: key account managers and frontline sales can spend around 70% of their time preparing internally for buyer meetings rather than the sales process
insights.locator: Yet in many organizations, the opposite happens.

insights.claim: Every commercial capability CPG companies built over the past decade — revenue growth management, category development, e-commerce, shopper insights — was designed to add retailer value but each layer added internal handoffs and coordination loops, producing a paradox where more capability yields less customer-facing time.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Capability investments in CPG have been value-destroying at the margin without an operating-model change — a reason to discount management claims that new commercial functions will unlock growth.
insights.quote: But each layer added internal handoffs, alignment meetings, and coordination loops. The result is a paradox
insights.locator: Yet in many organizations, the opposite happens.

insights.claim: Three specific dynamics keep CPG organizations inward-looking: using internal alignment as risk management (no one wants to contradict a colleague in front of a buyer), inward-looking functional metrics where RGM defends margin, key accounts defend volume and category management pushes category KPIs, and mistaking organizational complexity for sophistication.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: A concrete diagnostic checklist for judging whether a CPG's transformation program is real or cosmetic — look for changed metrics and decision rights, not new functions.
insights.quote: The first is the use of alignment as risk management.
insights.locator: Three dynamics keep this internal gravity in place.

insights.claim: CPG investments in new tools and data platforms have suffered low internal adoption because the tools sit outside the natural flow of work and add steps, so the output has been more dashboards rather than more alignment.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: A cautionary read-through for enterprise analytics and commercial-software vendors selling into CPG: seat-based deployments without workflow embedding churn; workflow-native and agentic products capture the budget.
insights.quote: The result is more dashboards, not more alignment.
insights.locator: Most CPG companies also have large volumes of data

insights.claim: CPG companies have strong functional experts but few leaders able to coordinate across functions, leaving teams facing misaligned leadership expectations and inconsistent cross-functional support.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity in integrative commercial leadership is a real execution constraint — transformation timelines at CPG issuers should be haircut accordingly.
insights.locator: Another issue is that many companies may have strong functional experts

insights.claim: The customer-back model designs the commercial organization backward from three specific retailer decision points that determine the year — the category story, the joint business plan (JBP), and the joint performance review — rather than from internal brand plans.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable operating definition: ask CPG managements whether their planning calendar is reverse-engineered from customer milestones or from their own fiscal cycle.
insights.quote: designing the commercial model backward from the three key decision points that determine the year with each retail customer: the category story, the joint business plan (JBP), and the joint performance review
insights.locator: This "customer-back" approach is more than a mindset

insights.claim: The stated target of a customer-back organization is to invert the time ratio so customer-facing teams spend roughly 80% of their time with customers rather than inside their own building.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: A measurable KPI to hold transformation programs to — time-with-customer is far harder to game than restructuring headcount charges.
insights.quote: the target is for customer-facing teams to spend roughly 80% of their time with customers, not inside their own building
insights.locator: A customer-back organization inverts that ratio

insights.claim: According to the Journal of Business Research, category leaders that co-develop plans with retailers deliver two to three times faster volume recovery than those relying on brand-led promotions.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Quantified payoff for joint planning versus promotional push — relevant when assessing which CPG names will recover volume fastest coming out of the price-led cycle.
insights.quote: category leaders that co-develop plans with retailers deliver two to three times faster volume recovery than those relying on brand-led promotions
insights.locator: In our experience, companies that shift to a customer-back approach

insights.claim: A customer-back business organizes around the profit pool it shares with retailers rather than around individual functional P&L line items, creating transparency on which customers, categories and initiatives genuinely create value from commercial spending.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Shared-profit-pool accounting reframes trade spend from a cost to defend to an investment to allocate — a lens for spotting CPGs with unproductive trade budgets.
insights.locator: A Corrective for Our Times

insights.claim: The recommended structural unit is a cross-functional 'customer pod' — category development, RGM, sales finance and supply orchestrated by the key account manager — that presents to the retailer as one story, one plan and one P&L instead of a parade of functional handoffs.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Pod structures imply one integrated plan per top retailer and one trade-off forum — a visible organizational signal that a CPG transformation is structural rather than rhetorical.
insights.quote: a cross-functional "customer pod" that shows up to the retailer as a single coordinated entity with one story, one plan, and one P&L
insights.locator: Develop a cross-functional commercial backbone.

insights.claim: Revenue growth management is cast as the only function with line of sight across pricing, promotion, mix and trade investment, making it the internal arbiter that can challenge sales' demand for deeper promotions, marketing's premium positioning and finance's margin protection against a single joint P&L.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Elevates RGM from a pricing analytics team to a governance function — where RGM reports and how much authority it holds becomes a meaningful organizational tell.
insights.quote: it's the only function with the line of sight to challenge any team's version of the story
insights.locator: The RGM team plays a key role in this process.

insights.claim: The key account manager's role is redefined from negotiator of price to orchestrator of joint value, walking into buyer meetings with a single pre-signed-off position rather than choosing among competing internal narratives based on what the buyer will accept.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Implies a materially different KAM skill and comp profile (financial acumen, co-value creation) — a hiring and training signal for CPG commercial organizations.
insights.quote: elevated from a negotiator of price to an orchestrator of joint value
insights.locator: The most visible change is in the role of the key account manager

insights.claim: In the strongest customer-back cases, retailers come to view a manufacturer's absence from strategic discussions as a competitive disadvantage and invite them in earlier with their toughest challenges.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Describes the end-state moat in a world where data advantage has eroded: partnership indispensability rather than information asymmetry.
insights.quote: customers should come to see a manufacturer's absence as a competitive disadvantage
insights.locator: Real Benefits Await

themes.theme: Connected data loops and agentic AI in trade

insights.claim: Connected decision loops let teams move from arguing over whose number is correct to isolating causes — separating volume from mix, price from promotion, distribution gaps from execution gaps, and category headwinds from share losses — so root causes surface within days and can be corrected before the next planning cycle locks in the same mistake.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Cycle-time of diagnosis becomes a competitive variable; firms that can re-plan intra-cycle will show less volatile quarterly execution than peers.
insights.quote: root causes surface in a matter of days and corrective action can be taken before the next cycle locks in the same mistakes
insights.locator: Crucially, connected loops can also improve the diagnosis

insights.claim: AI and analytics that remove repetitive preparation work can free 20% to 30% of time in CPG commercial roles, and when that reclaimed time is reinvested into customer engagement it produces, in BCG's experience, a 1- to 3-percentage-point uplift in annual revenue.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: This is the explicit AI-to-P&L bridge for consumer goods: the value is claimed on the revenue line via redeployed selling time, not in headcount cuts — test management AI claims against revenue, not cost.
insights.quote: a 20% to 30% gain in time translates into stronger partnerships and, in our experience, a 1- to 3-percentage-point uplift in annual revenue
insights.locator: A successful implementation results in a meaningful redistribution of time.

insights.claim: The next step beyond analytics is agentic AI for account teams: a single assistant that consolidates a 360-degree account view, monitors performance against plan and flags deviations, drafts the first version of a customer review or JBP from live data, runs pricing and promo simulations against live retailer constraints, and prepares negotiation scenarios with supporting evidence.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Defines a concrete near-term enterprise agentic-AI use case with measurable ROI — a demand pocket for trade-promotion, RGM and account-planning software vendors.
insights.quote: tools that don't just surface insights but take action across the workflow
insights.locator: The next step on this path is agentic AI

insights.claim: Tools should be built around workflows rather than functions, which simplifies the overall technology stack because each tool serves a clear purpose in the planning process rather than adding another layer.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Points to consolidation of CPG commercial software spend toward fewer workflow-native platforms and away from point-solution dashboards.
insights.quote: The tools are built around workflows rather than functions
insights.locator: A successful implementation results in a meaningful redistribution of time.

insights.claim: Decision loops should be extended to the retailer by sharing performance signals such as retail margins and category sales growth, which builds trust and makes customer conversations forward-looking rather than debates about whose numbers are right.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Data transparency toward customers is being reframed from a risk to a relationship asset — a reversal of the traditional CPG posture of hoarding insight.
insights.locator: These decision loops should extend to customers as well.

insights.claim: Customer-back leadership requires installing leaders who have personally held commercial roles and will engage directly with retailers, join store walks and participate in joint reviews, rather than managing the customer relationship at arm's length.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: An observable management-quality screen: whether senior CPG executives are visibly present in customer forums and store-level work.
insights.locator: Embed customer-back into leadership and culture.

insights.claim: Companies should invest in capability hubs that supply markets with consistent expertise in sales, RGM, category management and analytics, explicitly bridging the global-to-local gap so standards apply consistently across geographies.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Centralized capability hubs are the countermeasure to the cross-border price-referencing threat from international buying groups — a structural response to a structural pricing risk.
insights.locator: Note that talent and capabilities matter as much as leadership skills.

insights.claim: Governance must assign clear decision rights and simple escalation paths so internal disagreements are settled quickly instead of being carried into customer conversations.
insights.speaker: Jean-Sébastien Verwaerde
insights.so_what: Decision rights, not org charts, are the binding constraint — a practical test of whether a restructuring will actually change commercial outcomes.
insights.locator: Companies also need to ensure that governance provides clear decision rights
